text: Mom dropped it at Sunday dinner like a fork hitting tile. Converting. My fork froze halfway up. The kitchen lights went too bright, then too dim, then somewhere wrong. My hands wouldn't sit still in my lap, kept finding the napkin, the tablecloth, the edge of the plate. I opened my mouth. Closed it. Opened it again. Nothing came out except a small, wet sound.

text: Renee gripped the back of the dining chair until her knuckles whitened. Her brother had said the words twice now and she still couldn't make them mean anything. Easter. Christmas. The room narrowed to the centerpiece, a wax pear nobody had ever liked. She wanted to leave. She wanted to sit down. topic: A family member announces they're converting to a different religion
text: Marcus listened to his daughter explain over coffee, her hands steady, his suddenly not. The mug rattled when he set it down. He nodded because his mouth wasn't ready. Forty years of mass. The smoke alarm started going off. I stood under it like it was the same kind of alarm as the one in my chest. I didn't move.

topic: A person finds out they were adopted through a DNA test
text: Theo opened his ancestry results in his car at lunch. The percentages didn't match anything his parents had said. There was a notification. New close family match. He clicked. A first cousin he'd never heard of. He scrolled to the family tree. He tried to make the names mean something. None did. The car was warm. Too warm. He turned the key. He didn't drive anywhere. He sat. His hand on the steering wheel was unsteady. He thought about his mother. He thought about his father. He scrolled the tree again. The names were still not his.

topic: A person finds out they were adopted through a DNA test
text: I clicked the email at my desk and saw the percentages and forgot how to be at work. The Italian I'd grown up celebrating wasn't there. None of it. The match list at the bottom had a half-sister. A half-sister. My boss walked by and asked if I had a minute. I said yes. I'm pretty sure I said yes. I followed her into the meeting room. I sat in the chair. She started talking and her words slid past me. My hand on the table had a low constant tremor. I nodded at the wrong times. I nodded too much.

topic: A person finds out they were adopted through a DNA test
text: Petra opened the app on her phone in line at the post office. The results loaded. The results were wrong. They had to be wrong. She refreshed. They weren't wrong. The genetic match was zero percent for the heritage she'd grown up claiming. The line moved. She didn't move. The clerk called next. She didn't go. The person behind her went past her. She stepped to the side. She read the percentages again. The breakdown was for a part of the world she'd never associated with herself. Her hand on the phone wouldn't quite still itself.

topic: A person finds out they were adopted through a DNA test
text: I called my sister to share my fun results and started reading and stopped halfway. The numbers didn't make sense. We had completely different ethnic breakdowns. Completely. We weren't actually full siblings. I knew that immediately. She kept saying are you there. I was on the floor of my bedroom. I'd sat down without remembering sitting down. The phone was loud. Her voice was loud. My own voice was small. I said the numbers out loud. I said them again. She went quiet. I said her name. She said yeah. Neither of us said anything for a long time.

topic: Someone finds out they have a half-sibling they never knew about
text: Marcus opened the message. A woman with his last name and his father's eyes wanted to know if he was who she thought he was. He looked at her profile picture. The picture looked like his daughter. The picture looked like him. He sat down on the kitchen floor. The kitchen floor was tile. The tile was cold. He'd been holding a banana. He set the banana down on the floor. He picked the banana up. He set it down. He read the message again. The picture didn't change. He scrolled to her bio. He scrolled back to the picture.

topic: Someone finds out they have a half-sibling they never knew about
text: She emailed me at work. The subject line had my mother's name. I opened it. She thought we might be sisters. She had a photograph of my mom from before I was born. Her father was someone I'd never heard of. My screen blurred. The office around me kept being an office. Someone laughed at the printer. I stood up. I sat down. I stood up. I went to the bathroom and washed my hands without using soap. I looked at my face in the mirror. My face had pieces of someone I'd never met in it. Maybe. Probably.

topic: Someone finds out they have a half-sibling they never knew about
text: Lin received a letter from a half-brother she had not known existed. The letter was three pages, handwritten. She read it on the porch. The porch swing creaked. Her hand on the paper started to do the thing hands do. Her father had died ten years ago. Her father had not told her. Her mother was inside watching TV. She would have to ask her mother. She would have to ask her mother today. She folded the letter. Unfolded it. Folded it. She stood up. The swing kept moving without her. She walked toward the door. She turned around.

topic: Someone finds out they have a half-sibling they never knew about
text: I matched with her on a DNA site as a half-sibling and stared at the screen for ten minutes. We had the same father. The father I'd buried last year. She was three years older than me. Three. Which meant. I tried not to do the math but I'd already done the math. The math was bad. My hand on the mouse went numb. I scrolled her profile. She was a pediatric nurse. She had a son. Her son had my father's nose. I closed the tab. Opened it. Closed it. I drank water. I drank more water.

topic: Someone finds out they have a half-sibling they never knew about
text: Devon got the call from a stranger who said her name was his sister. Devon's mom had given her up for adoption at sixteen. Devon hadn't known. Devon was twenty-seven. The phone was warm against his ear. He paced his apartment. He paced into the kitchen. He paced into the bedroom. He sat on the bed. Stood up. Sat down. The woman on the phone was patient. She had been waiting decades. Devon was a person who'd had two days' notice. His voice came out wrong. He said her name. He said it wrong. He said it right. He said it wrong again.

topic: Someone learns their favorite author plagiarized their stories
text: I was rereading my favorite novel for the fifth time and I hit a paragraph that was familiar. Not familiar from this book. Familiar from another book. I pulled the other book off my shelf. The paragraph was almost identical. I checked another page. Another. The whole middle section. I sat on the floor of my apartment surrounded by both books and my hands started to do a thing. This author had been my favorite for a decade. A decade. I'd recommended the book in my wedding toast. My wedding toast. I closed both books. I opened them. I closed them.

topic: Someone learns their favorite author plagiarized their stories
text: Ines saw the news in a literary blog. Her favorite author. Plagiarism. Receipts. She clicked. The receipts were thorough. The receipts were not deniable. She'd written her senior thesis on this author. Her senior thesis. She closed the laptop. Opened it. The article was still there. She'd attended three readings. She'd waited in line for a signed book. She still had the signed book. She walked over to her shelf. She pulled the book down. She held it. She put it back. She pulled it down. She put it back. She sat in the chair across from her shelf and stared.

topic: Someone learns their favorite author plagiarized their stories
text: My book club was discussing him tonight. Tonight. I'd planned the snacks. I opened Twitter on the train and the whole feed was about him. The plagiarism. I clicked an article. Then another. The evidence kept stacking. I missed my stop. I rode three more stations. I got off and walked back. My phone in my hand had a tremor. The book club was at my house in two hours. The snacks were in my fridge. The book was on my coffee table. I was supposed to lead the discussion. I'd written notes. The notes now said nothing useful.

topic: Someone learns their favorite author plagiarized their stories
text: Reuben got a Google alert. His favorite living writer was being accused. He read the article. The accusations were specific. He pulled up his Kindle. He opened the most recent novel. He searched a phrase he remembered from another writer's work. The search hit. He searched another phrase. Another hit. His tablet got heavy. He set it down on the kitchen island. He picked it up. He set it down. The mug of coffee next to him was steaming and cold all at once. He picked up the mug. His hand was visibly unsteady. He set it down.

topic: Someone learns their favorite author plagiarized their stories
text: I got the Substack notification while I was making dinner. I clicked. The screenshots loaded. Side by side. Her words next to another author's words. Identical sentences. Identical. topic: A traveler's flight is delayed, causing them to miss an important event
text: Solene watched the gate agent change the status to canceled. Her cousin's wedding was tomorrow. She was the maid of honor. She held her boarding pass. The boarding pass was useless. topic: A traveler's flight is delayed, causing them to miss an important event
text: The board changed. Three hours added to the delay. My presentation was at six. I needed to land at four to make it. I would now land at seven. My hands went cold. I walked to the gate agent. I walked back. The terminal was a corridor. The corridor felt long. I called my colleague. She picked up. I tried to tell her and the words came out the wrong order. I started over. The PA system announced something I didn't catch. I stopped to listen. I missed it. I asked the woman next to me what they'd said. She didn't know either.

topic: A traveler's flight is delayed, causing them to miss an important event
text: Antonio realized at the gate that the connection was already gone. He hadn't even left the first city. The agent was apologetic. The next available flight was in eleven hours. topic: A traveler's flight is delayed, causing them to miss an important event
text: I was watching the runway through the window when the captain came on. Mechanical issue. We needed to deplane. My daughter's recital was tonight. Her first solo. I'd promised. I'd promised. topic: A traveler's flight is delayed, causing them to miss an important event
text: Jenna refreshed the airline app. Delayed. Delayed. Delayed. Her sister's funeral was at ten in the morning. She had been on the way for sixteen hours. The latest delay was four hours. topic: A neighbor's dog keeps escaping into their yard
text: Reyna heard the screaming and ran outside. The dog had her cat cornered against the fence. The dog was big. The cat was thirteen. Reyna picked up the rake. The rake was heavy. She didn't know what to do with the rake. She was shouting. She wasn't sure what she was shouting. The dog turned and looked at her. The dog turned back to the cat. Reyna stepped forward. She stepped back. She stepped forward. Her hands on the rake were trembling. The cat hissed. The dog growled. The neighbor was nowhere. She'd told the neighbor twice this month.

topic: A neighbor's dog keeps escaping into their yard
text: I came outside with my coffee and the dog was on my porch. Again. My toddler was inside, two feet from the screen door. The screen door was not strong. The dog was big and the dog had a history. My coffee fell. I didn't see it fall. I just heard it. I picked up my toddler. He was confused. The dog wagged its tail. I wasn't reassured. topic: A neighbor's dog keeps escaping into their yard
text: Walter found the chickens scattered. Four were missing. The dog from next door was standing in the middle of his garden, mouth bloody. Walter dropped the egg basket. The eggs cracked. He held it anyway. His phone was in his pocket. His pocket suddenly seemed far. He fumbled it out. He dropped it in the dirt. He picked it up. He dialed wrong.

topic: A neighbor's dog keeps escaping into their yard
text: The dog was in my yard with my kid's tricycle in its mouth. My five-year-old was in the sandbox. The dog dropped the tricycle and looked at my five-year-old. I yelled. I'm not sure what I yelled. My slippers were on. The grass was wet. I half-ran half-slipped across the lawn. The dog's tail wagged. I'd seen that wag before. I'd also seen what came after. I scooped up my kid. My kid was heavy and confused. I kept the dog in my peripheral vision. I backed up to the door. I dropped the keys. I dropped them again.

topic: A neighbor's dog keeps escaping into their yard
text: Inez stepped onto her deck and the dog was already there, tongue out, watching her cat through the sliding door. The cat was on the other side of the glass, fur up. Inez set her tea down too hard. The mug cracked. She didn't see the crack. She tried to remember the dog's name. She couldn't. She tried to call her neighbor. Her phone was inside. Her phone was on the kitchen counter. Her cat was on the deck side of the door. Her hand on the door handle wouldn't decide. Slide it open. Don't slide it open. Slide it. Don't.

topic: A person accidentally sends a text to the wrong recipient
text: I was venting to my best friend about my boss. I called him a name. A real name. I hit send. The conversation thread was open. I looked at the top. The thread was not my best friend. The thread was my boss. My boss. I tried to delete it. The delete only deletes on my end. He'd already seen it. He was always on his phone. My ears went so hot the rest of my face followed. I started typing an explanation. I deleted it. Started again. Deleted it. My screen got blurry. The message was still there at the top of the thread.

topic: A person accidentally sends a text to the wrong recipient
text: Daniela meant to send the photo to her sister. The photo was her at a doctor's office holding a positive pregnancy test. The text went to her group chat. Her in-laws were in the group chat. Her husband had not yet been told. She watched the read receipts populate. One. Two. Three. She sat down on the bathroom floor. She stood up. She sat down. She tried to type but her hands were not following directions. The chat exploded with replies. Her phone was vibrating constantly. She covered the screen with her hand like that would help. It did not.

topic: A person accidentally sends a text to the wrong recipient
text: I sent my mom a screenshot of a Tinder match. To my mom. I had been showing my friend. The thread above it was my mom because we'd been planning Sunday dinner. I saw the send go through and watched the little delivered icon change to read. Read. Read fast. My mom was a fast reader. My laptop was open and I closed the laptop for no reason. I opened my phone. My phone was not the laptop. My hand on the phone was unsteady. The typing dots from her appeared. The dots stopped. The dots started. The dots stopped.

topic: A person accidentally sends a text to the wrong recipient
text: Kasim was drafting a long complaint about his landlord. He hit send. The recipient was, in fact, his landlord. He stared at his phone. The message was a wall of text. He tried to recall the message. There was no recall. He sat down on his couch. He stood up. He sat down. The landlord was probably reading it now. The landlord, who renewed leases yearly. Kasim's stomach dropped. He started to type an apology. He stopped. He started again. The first version was groveling. The second version was worse. He sent neither. The dots from the landlord appeared.

topic: A person accidentally sends a text to the wrong recipient
text: I texted my crush a message about my crush. About him. The message went to him. To him. The recipient name at the top was unmistakable now that I was looking. I'd been texting my best friend on the previous thread. I locked the phone. I unlocked it. The message was still there. The dots appeared. Oh god. The dots stopped. The dots appeared again. I stood up. I sat down. I stood up. The dots stopped. They didn't come back. I waited. I waited. Then a single word came back, and I read it about seven times in a row.

topic: A person learns their college is closing down
text: Ji-won got the email at six in the morning. The subject said Important Update. The body said the college would close at the end of the academic year. She was a junior. Her credits might transfer. They might not. She was in her dorm bed. She sat up. The mattress springs squeaked. Her roommate stirred. Ji-won got out of bed. She paced the room. The room was small. She paced into the bathroom. She paced back. Her phone kept buzzing. The group chats were already going. She read three messages. She put the phone down. She picked it up.

topic: A person learns their college is closing down
text: The president's email landed during my biology lecture. I read it under the desk. The college was closing. May. May. I had a senior thesis to write. My thesis advisor would not exist. The lecture continued. I couldn't hear the lecture. I packed up. I unpacked. I packed up. I walked out. The hallway lighting was the wrong yellow. I went outside. The campus was a campus. The trees I'd grown to recognize. The bench by the chapel. The ridiculous fountain. All of it would be sold. My ears were ringing. My hands were ice. I sat on the bench.

topic: A person learns their college is closing down
text: Walden was at his work-study job at the library when his phone lit up. Three texts. Then five. Then twelve. He pulled out his phone. The college was closing in May. He stood at the desk. The patron in front of him was waiting. Walden tried to scan the book. The scanner missed. He tried again. He missed. The patron was being patient. Walden's hands were shaking. He read the email. He read it again. He scanned the book. He gave the book back. He sat down on the stool behind the desk. He stood up. He sat down.

topic: A person learns their college is closing down
text: I'd just paid my deposit for next year. I read the email and laughed. The wrong kind of laugh. My financial aid package. My friends. The professor who'd written my recommendation letters. All of it dissolving. I was in the cafeteria. The cafeteria was loud. People were starting to react. A girl two tables over started crying. Two boys started yelling. I stood up. I sat down. I stood up. I left my tray. I came back for it. I dropped my fork. I picked it up. I left my tray again. I walked outside. I walked back inside.

topic: A person learns their college is closing down
text: Bea was on a study abroad in Madrid when she saw the news. The college was closing. She was a sophomore. She read the email twice in her host family's kitchen. The host mother offered her toast. Bea declined. She accepted. She didn't eat the toast. She walked into her room. The room was small and pink. She sat on the bed. She stood up. She sat down. Her plane ticket home was for July. The college would not exist in July. She'd planned to graduate from this college. She'd planned. The bed creaked under her shifting weight.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: The nurse called and started reading me results that weren't mine. Cholesterol numbers I'd never had. A medication I'd never taken. A diagnosis I'd never been given. I was at my desk at work. I stood up. The chair rolled away. The cubicle wall didn't hold me. I held the phone too tight. I said wait. I said wait three times. She kept reading. I said stop. She stopped. The records had my name. The records were not me. Or worse, my records were somewhere being read to someone else. My hand on the phone was a tremor.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: Petra logged into her patient portal and saw lab results she didn't recognize. A blood test she hadn't taken. A diagnosis she'd never received. She scrolled. There were more. Imaging from a body part she'd never had imaged. Her hand on the mouse went tight. She refreshed. The records were still there. She closed the laptop. Opened it. The records were still there. She picked up the phone. Set it down. Picked it up. Dialed the clinic. The hold music started. The hold music kept going. She paced into the kitchen. She paced into the bedroom. She paced back.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: I went in for a routine checkup and the doctor opened my file and started talking about my heart condition. I don't have a heart condition. I told her. She frowned. She scrolled. She kept scrolling. The medications listed weren't my medications. The surgeries weren't my surgeries. Someone else's life was on my chart. Mine was where. I sat up on the exam table. The paper crinkled. I tried to ask her a calm question and produced a half-coherent sentence. She told me to wait. She left the room. The door closed. I sat there. The room was the wrong room.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: Rashid got a call from a pharmacy about a prescription he didn't order. The pharmacist read off the medication. It was a high-dose blood thinner. Rashid was not on a blood thinner. The pharmacist apologized. Rashid did not feel apologized to. He said he'd call the doctor. He hung up. He paced his kitchen. He sat. He stood. He sat. If they had records that wrong, what else was wrong. What had they given him before that they shouldn't have. What had they not given him that they should have. He picked up the phone again. He dialed the wrong number.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: I got an EOB from my insurance for a procedure I never had. I read the description three times. A biopsy. A biopsy. I had not had a biopsy. The provider was a doctor I'd seen once. The date was last month. My hand on the paper was shaking enough that the paper trembled. I called insurance. They said it had gone through. I called the doctor's office. They put me on hold. The hold music was instrumental. Smooth. Mocking. I paced. I sat. I paced. The receptionist came back and said someone would call me back.
